definition: Paucity means an amount of something so small it is strikingly close to none.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word paucity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know paucity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum's dinosaur hall is grand, but its paucity of actual fossils - four, by the docent's count - disappoints visitors expecting a herd.
A shortage says supply has slipped below need and may recover next week; paucity is bleaker - strikingly, countably few.
Absence goes past paucity: paucity means almost none, while absence means none at all - even the last few are gone.

Scarcity is the economist's neutral word for supply running short of demand, at any degree from mild to severe. Paucity is never mild: it insists the numbers are stark, strikingly close to none. A scarcity of taxis means a longer wait; a paucity means the street stays empty.

A shortfall is the measured amount by which a target is missed — it needs a number to miss. Paucity needs no target at all: it simply says that what is present is strikingly, countably small, whatever anyone planned or promised.

A dearth is a serious lack of something needed — the word points at the unmet need. Paucity points at the count itself: not merely lacking, but strikingly, almost absurdly few. A dearth of volunteers means too few came; a paucity means you can name them all.

so much that the excess itself becomes the problem

Latin paucus, 'few,' never became an English adjective, so paucity stands alone - there are no working parts to peel off. Its kin are distant: poor and pauper grew from the same ancient root for 'little,' but by separate paths, so the family resemblance is faint.
Paucity means an amount of something so small it is strikingly close to none.
The relief coordinator's inventory was blunt: nine hundred evacuees, forty cots.
It was the paucity of blankets that worried her most, though - the forecast called for frost, and the shelf held eleven.
Paucity is 'too few' with the volume turned up: not merely 'less than we'd like' but strikingly, almost absurdly few.
A shortage can be mild; paucity invites you to count on your fingers - forty cots, eleven blankets - and feel the gap.
Paucity is essay-and-report vocabulary, nearly always followed by 'of': a paucity of data, of witnesses, of options.
In conversation, say 'hardly any.' Choose paucity over shortage when the fewness is stark and you want the reader to feel it, not just note it.

When the last fluent speaker of Werana died in 2011, the university's archive became the language's whole surviving body.
The catalog lists eleven minutes of tape: two songs, a folktale broken by static, and a shopping list recited as a grammar demonstration.
Linguists trying to reconstruct the verb system speak of the paucity of material the way climbers speak of thin air — every step of analysis must be made on almost nothing.
By contrast, neighboring languages left hundreds of hours; students of those tongues discard more recordings than Werana's specialists will ever possess.
A grammar of Werana was published last year anyway.
Its preface thanks the folktale's teller by name, twice.
